Symmetric encryption using AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 protects application data. Message authentication codes prevent tampering. Session resumption using PSK or session tickets reduces subsequent handshake overhead. TLS 1.3 removed vulnerable features like RSA key exchange and CBC cipher suites, improving security and performance compared to TLS 1.2.
sections.title: TLS Handshake and Cryptography

sections.content: Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) provides trust model for certificate validation. Certificate Authorities (CA) issue certificates after validating domain ownership through DNS, HTTP, or email challenges. Let's Encrypt provides free automated certificates through ACME protocol, revolutionizing certificate accessibility. Certificate validity periods balance security (shorter periods limit exposure) with operational overhead. Certificate chains include end-entity certificate, intermediate certificates, and root CA certificate trusted by clients. Subject Alternative Names (SAN) enable single certificate covering multiple domains. Wildcard certificates cover all subdomains of a domain. Certificate pinning in mobile apps validates against known certificates, preventing MITM attacks from rogue CAs. Certificate Transparency logs publicly record all issued certificates, enabling detection of unauthorized issuance. OCSP and CRL provide certificate revocation checking, though OCSP stapling improves privacy and performance. Certificate renewal automation using cert-manager in Kubernetes or certbot on servers prevents expiration outages.
sections.title: Certificate Management and PKI

sections.content: Mutual TLS extends TLS with client certificate authentication, enabling strong identity verification for service-to-service communication. The mTLS handshake includes certificate request from server, with client sending certificate for validation. Client certificate validation verifies signature chain and checks revocation status. Service meshes like Istio or Linkerd automate mTLS, issuing short-lived certificates to service proxies. Zero trust architectures rely on mTLS for authenticating all network connections regardless of network location. Certificate rotation becomes critical with short-lived certificates, requiring automated renewal. SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone) provides standardized identity framework for workloads. SPIRE implements SPIFFE, issuing SVIDs (SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Documents) as X.509 certificates. mTLS eliminates need for network-based trust, enabling secure communication across untrusted networks. Performance overhead from TLS handshakes mitigated through connection pooling and session resumption. Certificate management complexity increases with scale, requiring automation and monitoring.
sections.title: Mutual TLS (mTLS) for Service Authentication

sections.content: Production TLS configuration requires attention to protocol versions, cipher suites, and security headers. Disable TLS 1.0 and 1.1, supporting only TLS 1.2 and 1.3. Configure strong cipher suites with forward secrecy (ECDHE, DHE), avoiding weak ciphers (RC4, 3DES). Use 2048-bit or 4096-bit RSA keys, or 256-bit ECDSA for better performance. Enable HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) forcing browsers to use HTTPS. Configure OCSP stapling reducing client-side revocation checking overhead. Implement certificate monitoring alerting on expiration, revocation, or configuration issues. Use tools like SSL Labs for configuration testing and recommendations. Monitor TLS handshake metrics including duration, failure rates, and version distribution. Log TLS errors for debugging and security investigation. Implement TLS termination at load balancers for centralized certificate management and performance. Re-encryption to backends provides end-to-end encryption in high-security environments. Regular security audits validate compliance with current best practices as vulnerabilities emerge.
sections.title: Configuration Best Practices and Monitoring
